wine.name: Lyrarakis Plyto Psarades
wine.grapes: Plyto alone, an old white grape of Crete that the family brought back from near loss.
wine.sites: The family's Psarades vineyard near Alagni in the hills of central Crete, at about 450 to 480 metres, where Plyto was first planted in 1992.
wine.making: The grapes are destemmed and lightly crushed, and by the house's own vintage sheets the method moves with the year: in some vintages part or all of the must spends from a few hours to two days on its skins before a cool fermentation, and in some years a share of the wine has a short spell in oak before bottling.
wine.glass: White peach, pear and lemon over a chalky, gently salty edge and a herbal finish; lively in acidity, with a slightly creamy texture in the mouth.
wine.ageing: Ready on release and at its liveliest in its first few years; the sources read here give it no long keeping life.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a white wine glass of moderate size.

label.means: The white grape, also written Plytó, which the Lyrarakis family saved from near loss.
The family vineyard near Alagni where the grape was planted in 1992.
The island's Protected Geographical Indication, wider than its seven appellations.

records.table: Lyrarakis Plyto Psarades is a white from a Cretan grape that had almost vanished until the family planted it in its Psarades vineyard near Alagni in 1992. Expect white peach, pear and a salty, herbal edge; pour it cool with grilled fish or seafood.
records.story: Two brothers of the Lyrarakis family founded the winery in 1966 at Alagni, a village in the hills south of Heraklion. As Crete replanted its vineyards in the decades that followed, the island's old local grapes gave way to more productive ones, and Plyto and Dafni, two whites of central Crete, came close to being lost. They were the first grapes the family set out to research, and in 1992 it planted both in its Psarades vineyard at almost 500 metres. The first wines of each grape alone followed in the 1990s. The house tells of long years of obstacles from state agencies before the old grapes could be planted and labelled freely; that is its own telling, and it adds that those restrictions have since almost vanished. A second generation took the work on, and Melissaki later joined Plyto and Dafni as a third old grape the house says it revived. Plyto carries the whole idea of the house: a grape nearly gone, kept alive in one family vineyard and poured again by the glass. For a sommelier it is the clearest case of Crete reviving its own white grapes, and a wine no other island can pour.

others.name: Lyrarakis Dafni Psarades

others.name: Lyrarakis Liatiko Aggelis

Dafni is a grape named for the laurel, a different thing from Dafnes, the village appellation near Heraklion.

cards.front: Plyto Psarades: from which grape is it made, and why does that grape matter?
cards.back: Plyto alone, an old white grape of Crete that the Lyrarakis family brought back from near loss.

A sweet wine from dried grapes
questions.exp: Psarades is the family's vineyard near Alagni where Plyto was planted in 1992; the wine is labelled PGI Crete, not a village appellation such as Dafnes or Peza.

questions.q: In what year was the Lyrarakis winery founded at Alagni, in the hills south of Heraklion?
questions.exp: Two brothers of the family founded the winery in 1966; 1930 is the start of Douloufakis at Dafnes and 1994 the founding of Domaine Economou in Sitia.

report: Searches for this record: six of the group's 35; no fetch tried.

The founding in 1966 by two brothers and the planting of Plyto and Dafni at Psarades in 1992 are the house's own pages, with Berry Bros and a Greek retailer beside them; the brothers are not named, since their dates were not found.
The year of the first single grape bottlings is 1996 in one writer's account and the early 1990s in another, so the story says the 1990s.

The soil of Psarades is clay loam on the house's sheet of 2018 and gravel over limestone in one visitor's account, so the soil is left out; the altitude is 480 metres on most sheets and 450 on one, so the record gives both.
The making changes vintage by vintage on the house's own sheets (skin contact from hours to two days, a short oak spell in some years), so the record tells the range and no single year.
Dafni could be argued the house's flagship as well; Plyto was kept as the plan's pick, since Berry Bros and the house both present it as the grape the family saved.

records.place: Dafnes, Heraklion, PGI Crete, central Crete, Greece

wine.name: Douloufakis Dafnios Vidiano
wine.grapes: Vidiano alone, an old white grape of Crete that the family began to plant again in 2000.
wine.sites: The family's own vineyards on the hill slopes around Dafnes, south of Heraklion, at about 350 to 450 metres.
wine.making: Made as a classic white: the juice is fermented in stainless steel tanks at about 18 degrees Celsius, and the wine sees no barrel in either fermentation or maturation before it is bottled, by the house's own sheet.
wine.glass: Yellow peach and orange zest over honey blossom, with a stony edge, juicy fruit and fresh, fine acidity that carries a long finish.
wine.ageing: Fresh and open on release; the house says it may be kept for up to five years.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, within the range the house gives for its Vidiano; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: Of Dafnes, the family's village; the name the house gives its white and red.
The white grape, an old Cretan variety brought back from near loss.
The island's Protected Geographical Indication, not the village appellation of Dafnes.

records.table: Douloufakis Dafnios Vidiano comes from the family's vineyards around Dafnes, south of Heraklion: an old Cretan white grape, fermented cool in steel and never put in oak. Expect yellow peach, orange zest and honey blossom; pour it cool with fish or Cretan greens.
records.story: The family's winemaking begins in 1930, when the founder, the grandfather of the present winemaker, began to make wine professionally in old premises at Dafnes, as the house tells it. His son took the winery on in 1960. Phylloxera reached Crete around 1977, by the house's account, and destroyed most of the island's vineyards; the replanting at Dafnes began in 1980 and lasted nearly a decade. The first bottled wines came in 1997, among them a red of Liatiko first released under the name Dafnes, the village's appellation. In 2000 the founder's grandson, of the third generation, turned to Vidiano, a white grape of Crete then close to extinction: he sought out the surviving vines and planted new vineyards, and the grape became the heart of the house's whites. Dafnios, the adjective of Dafnes, ties the wine to its village, and the white Dafnios is pure Vidiano made in steel. Other Cretan houses took up the grape over the same years, and Vidiano went from near loss to a white poured across the island and beyond it. For a sommelier the Dafnios is the plain, unoaked statement of the grape from the family that put it back in the ground.

others.name: Douloufakis Dafnios red
others.note: A red of Liatiko, first released in 1997 under the name Dafnes.

others.name: Douloufakis Aspros Lagos
others.note: A second white of Vidiano in the house's range.

traps: Dafnios is the house's name for its wines, from the village of Dafnes; the white is labelled PGI Crete, not PDO Dafnes.
Dafnios Vidiano is the white; the Dafnios red is Liatiko, a different grape and a different wine.

cards.front: Douloufakis: in what year did the family turn to the nearly lost Vidiano grape?

cards.front: Dafnios Vidiano: how much oak does it see?
cards.back: None: it is fermented in stainless steel at about 18 degrees Celsius, with no barrel at any stage.

questions.q: A guest asks what the word Dafnios on a Douloufakis label means. What is the true reply?
opts: It names the village of Dafnes
questions.exp: Dafnios is the adjective of Dafnes, the family's village south of Heraklion; the white is pure Vidiano, so the name has nothing to do with the Dafni grape.

questions.q: From what year does the Douloufakis family date its winemaking at Dafnes?
questions.exp: The house dates its winemaking to 1930; 1997 brought its first bottled wines and 2000 its turn to Vidiano, while 1966 is the founding of Lyrarakis.

report: Searches for this record: four of the group's 35; no fetch tried.

The dates 1930, 1960, 1977, 1980, 1997 and 2000 are the house's own history page; 1930 and the grandson's turn to Vidiano are matched by two trade listings, and the family is described, not named, since no dates were found.
The grandson's relation is read from the house's sequence and a trade listing that calls him the third generation; a refuter may wish to confirm it.
The tasting note rests on one critic's published note and the importers' sheets; a second note was read in a source whose address names a living writer, so it is not cited.
One listing gives 2005 as a first release, without saying of which wine, so no first vintage of the Dafnios white is given; the estate's size differs between sources and is left out as volatile.
The house's serving range for Vidiano is 9 to 12 degrees Celsius and 9 to 10 on the Dafnios sheet; the record gives 9 to 11.

wine.name: Oikonomoy Sitia Liatiko
wine.grapes: Liatiko, the great majority and at least four fifths by the Sitia rules, from a local clone of the plateau, with a little Mandilaria in some vintages.
wine.sites: Old vines, many on their own roots, around Ziros, Katsidoni and Etia on the Ziros plateau above Sitia, at about 600 to 650 metres.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts in stainless steel after about a week on the skins, then aged in oak, sixteen months in Burgundian casks of 350 litres in one vintage and two years in French oak before years more in steel in another, by merchants' notes. The estate releases a vintage only when it judges it ready, often a decade or more after the harvest.
wine.glass: Pale garnet turning brick at the rim; orange peel, sour red cherry and thyme, with fine, dry tannin and fresh acidity carried through long age.
wine.ageing: Released already mature, often a decade or more after the harvest; it is ready when poured and keeps for some years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant gently off any sediment shortly before serving; a Burgundy glass for its perfume.

label.means: The PDO of eastern Crete; its red is at least four fifths Liatiko, the rest Mandilaria.
The family name as the label prints it, written Economou or Oikonomou elsewhere.
The pale red grape of Crete on which the estate built its reds.

records.table: Domaine Economou's Sitia Liatiko comes from old vines on the Ziros plateau in the far east of Crete and is released only when the estate thinks it ready, often a decade after the harvest. Pale and mature, with orange peel, red cherry and thyme, it suits roast lamb.
records.story: The estate stands on the Ziros plateau above Sitia, at the eastern end of Crete, where the family had kept old vines, many on their own roots. Its founder studied oenology in Italy and worked in Germany, in Bordeaux at Château Margaux and in Piedmont before he came home in 1994 and began to make wine from the family's vineyards, as the accounts of the estate tell it. He built the reds on the plateau's own clone of Liatiko, a pale red grape, and treated it as a wine for long keeping: ageing in oak, then years in tank and bottle at the estate before release. The winery keeps no fixed release calendar, so its vintages reach the market when they are ready rather than in order: the 2004 Sitia spent two years in oak and several more in steel vats before it was sold, and the 2006 came to American shelves only after earlier vintages had. Sitia's appellation calls for at least four fifths Liatiko in its red, with Mandilaria beside it. The estate also makes a white of Thrapsathiri, Odyssey, and a sweet Liatiko from late picked grapes. For a sommelier its Sitia shows how a light Cretan red can age: a mature wine, ready when it is poured.

others.name: Economou Antigone
others.note: A red mainly of very old Liatiko vines, often with a little Mandilaria, given long ageing in large old oak.

others.name: Economou Odyssey
others.note: A white of Thrapsathiri, given long ageing before release.

others.name: Economou Late Harvest Liatiko
others.note: A sweet red of late picked Liatiko from Sitia, aged for years in oak casks.

traps: Economou's Sitia is a dry red of Liatiko; the estate's sweet Liatiko is a separate late harvest wine.
The family name is printed Oikonomoy on the label and written Economou or Oikonomou elsewhere; it is one estate.

cards.front: Domaine Economou: where do its vineyards lie?
cards.back: On the Ziros plateau above Sitia in eastern Crete, at about 600 to 650 metres.

cards.front: Economou Sitia Liatiko: when does the estate release a vintage?

questions.q: A guest asks how much of a red PDO Sitia, such as Economou's, must be Liatiko. What is the rule?
questions.exp: The Sitia red is at least 80 per cent Liatiko, with up to a fifth Mandilaria; two thirds is too low a share for the appellation.

questions.q: Before he founded Domaine Economou in 1994, its founder worked at which Bordeaux estate?
questions.exp: The accounts of the estate place him at Château Margaux, between work in Germany and in Piedmont; Latour, Lafite and Haut-Brion are other first growths.

report: Searches for this record: five of the group's 35; no fetch tried. The estate has no website, so no primary page of its own was read.
The founding in 1994, the training in Italy and the work at Château Margaux rest on two trade sources; the founder is living and not named.

The making is given as merchants' notes on two vintages (2004 and 2006), since the estate publishes no sheet; a native yeast fermentation and 350 litre casks rest on one blog note, hedged as merchants' notes.

One source says the estate had the Sitia rules changed from the 2012 vintage so that its reds may be pure Liatiko, while the appellation summaries give at least 80 per cent Liatiko from 2012; the record keeps the rule of four fifths and leaves the claim out.
The vineyard area differs widely between sources (seven, fourteen, sixteen and almost twenty hectares) and is left out as volatile.
The tasting note draws on two notes of the 2004 and 2006 Sitia; one of them sits on a site whose address names a living writer and is not cited.
The plan's label was confirmed as the Sitia red of Liatiko; one menu site names Antigone the flagship, so Antigone goes in others, and a refuter may weigh which leads.

wine.name: Alexakis Vidiano
wine.grapes: Vidiano alone, the old white grape of Crete.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the Heraklion district at about 550 metres, on sandy clay rich in calcium, by the house's own account.
wine.making: The grapes are held for about a day at very low temperature and the juice is given some eight hours of cold contact with the skins; it is then fermented in stainless steel tanks for fifteen to twenty days, never above 16 degrees Celsius, by the house's own account of its Vidiano.
wine.glass: Peach and apricot over pear, lime zest and a grassy note, with a flinty edge and a gently bitter, peel like finish.
wine.ageing: A wine for its youth, poured within its first few years while the fruit is fresh; the sources read here give it no long keeping life.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The white grape of Crete, nearly abandoned before trial wines of the 1980s revived it.
The island's Protected Geographical Indication, covering wine from anywhere on Crete.

records.table: Alexakis Vidiano is Crete's revived white grape from a Heraklion family house that ships under its own name to America. Fermented cool in steel from vineyards at about 550 metres, it shows peach, apricot and a grassy freshness; pour it young and cool with seafood.
records.story: The house was founded in Heraklion in the 1970s by a chemical engineer and oenologist with his wife, and it has stayed a family business, run with their two sons, both oenologists, as the house tells it. It grew into what it calls the largest private winery on Crete, working with growers across the island. Vidiano, by the house's own history of the grape, had been grown on Crete for centuries and was nearly abandoned until producers began small trial vinifications in the 1980s; from them the grape came back to the vineyards of Heraklion and of Rethymno, where old vines on their own roots survive. The house made Vidiano one of its leading wines, and the island's producers' association names it among the house's ambassadors, beside a Kotsifali with Syrah and a white of Dafni. From 2008, by the house's account, it has exported to the United States under its own Alexakis name. A bottling of 2020 took a silver medal at the Decanter World Wine Awards of 2021, as the association reported. For a sommelier it is the widely found, approachable Vidiano: a first glass of the grape before the estate bottlings of Dafnes and Alagni.

others.name: Alexakis Kotsifali Syrah
others.note: A red of Crete's Kotsifali blended with Syrah, one of the house's export wines.

others.name: Alexakis Dafni
others.note: A white of the Dafni grape, named for the laurel.

traps: Vidiano and Vilana are different white grapes: Vilana is the older staple of Peza, Vidiano the revived grape of Heraklion and Rethymno.
Alexakis is a large family house working with growers across Crete, not a single vineyard estate like Douloufakis at Dafnes.

cards.front: Alexakis Vidiano: how is it fermented?

questions.q: Since what year has Alexakis exported to the United States under its own name?
questions.exp: The house dates its own brand in America to 2008; 1966 is the founding of Lyrarakis and 1994 that of Domaine Economou.

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35; no fetch tried.
No founding year beyond the 1970s was found in the house's pages or in the producers' association's, so founded is empty; the family is living and not named.
The making, the altitude and the soil rest on the house's own Vidiano page alone, read through search restricted to its domain; no importer sheet was found.
The tasting note joins the house's own words with a reprinted American review and a drinkers' app; a critic's note of no oak was read only on a site that names a living writer and is left out.
An American review reprinted by the association praises the wine in price terms; the record leaves that out under the house rule against price words.
The plan places the house at no village; the sources give its address as Peridi Metochi in Heraklion and none places it in Kounavi, a different house's village.

The pick is thin beside the estate Vidianos of Crete; a swap to a house with a published Vidiano sheet (Idaia, Silva Daskalaki or Diamantakis) could be weighed, but Alexakis is kept, since the producers' association and two export sources name its Vidiano among the grape's export bottlings.

records.place: Vatolakkos, near Chania, western Crete, Greece

wine.name: Manousakis Nostos Roussanne
wine.appellation: PGI Crete, or varietal wine of Greece by vintage
wine.grapes: Roussanne alone, the white grape of the Rhône, first planted here in 1993.
wine.sites: The family's organically farmed vineyards around Vatolakkos in the foothills of the Lefka Ori, the White Mountains, west of Chania; the first vines went in at about 350 metres.
wine.making: Fermented in French oak barrels and aged in them for about seven months before bottling, by the sheets of Greek merchants; the importer describes low yields and a slow fermentation.
wine.glass: Peach, apricot and honey over toast and vanilla from the oak, with a floral lift; full and rich in the mouth, with a long finish.
wine.ageing: Full and ready on release, with oak that shows in youth and settles over a few years; the sources read here give no firm keeping life.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a broad white wine glass, as for an oak aged white.

label.means: Greek for homecoming, the longing to return to one's homeland; the house's range name.
The white grape of the Rhône, planted here rather than a Cretan one.
The island's Protected Geographical Indication, printed on some vintages.

records.table: Manousakis Nostos Roussanne is a Rhône white grown in the foothills of the White Mountains near Chania, its name the Greek for homecoming. Fermented and aged in French oak, it is full and honeyed, with peach and apricot; pour it with roast chicken or rich fish.
records.story: The founder was born in Vatolakkos, a village near Chania in the west of Crete, and after years abroad he came back to make wine in his home village, as the family tells it. In 1993 the first vines went in, farmed organically, and they were not the island's own grapes but Roussanne, Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre of the Rhône, chosen on the advice of an American vine consultant. The family called the wines Nostos, the Greek for the longing to return home. In the summer of 1997, with the first harvest, it finished building its winery on the grounds of the family home, and the house tells that the surprise of that first year was how much fruit the Roussanne gave in Crete. The founder's daughter took up the winemaking in 2007, and the family later added Cretan and Greek grapes such as Romeiko and Assyrtiko beside the Rhône varieties. The Roussanne is the white the house is known by: a Rhône grape made into a full, oak aged white on a Mediterranean island. For a sommelier it is the counterpoint on a Cretan list, a house that began with France rather than with the island's revival of its own grapes.

others.name: Manousakis Nostos Blend
others.note: The red of the house: Syrah, Mourvèdre and Grenache, with a touch of Roussanne in some vintages.

others.name: Manousakis Nostos Pink
others.note: A dry rosé of Grenache, the Cretan Romeiko and Syrah.

traps: Nostos is the house's range name, Greek for homecoming, not a place or an appellation.
Roussanne is a Rhône grape, not a Cretan one; Manousakis planted Rhône varieties first and Cretan grapes only later.

cards.front: Manousakis Winery: what does its range name Nostos mean?
cards.back: Homecoming: the longing to return to one's homeland.

cards.front: Nostos Roussanne: in what year were the first vines planted at Vatolakkos?
cards.back: 1993, with Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre beside the Roussanne.

questions.q: A guest asks how Manousakis Nostos Roussanne is raised before bottling. What is the true reply?
opts: About seven months in French oak barrels
Two years in large old casks
Steel only, on its fine lees
In clay jars buried in the ground

questions.q: Which grapes did the Manousakis family first plant at Vatolakkos in 1993?
questions.exp: The first vines were Rhône varieties chosen on a consultant's advice; Cretan grapes such as Romeiko and Greek ones such as Assyrtiko came later.

report: Searches for this record: seven of the group's 35; no fetch tried. The plan's doubt is answered: the house, its village of Vatolakkos and its Nostos range are confirmed by its own pages, the producers' association and three trade sources.

The founding year is 1993 on the house's pages and in a Wine Enthusiast profile reprinted by the association; one retailer gives 1983 and one magazine 1984, the year the house says the dream began, so founded is 1993, the planting.
The founder, his daughter and the vine consultant are living and not named; the consultant's name appears on the house's page.
The appellation differs by vintage and seller: PGI Crete on two importers' sheets, Wine of Greece or varietal wine on two others, so the field says so; a refuter with a label in hand may settle it.
The seven months in French oak is two Greek merchants' sheets; no sheet of the house was read, and lees handling was found in no source.
The plan names Romeiko as the local red the house is known for; the only Romeiko wines found were the Nostos Pink and one listing of a white Romeiko, so Romeiko appears only in the story and others.
